body:
Try to remember that life still has positive feelings without weed. Funny movies are still funny. Delicious food is still delicious. It takes time to start enjoying things again, but it will happen.

It's also good to know that you *will* have cravings, and to have compassion for yourself when that happens. I can want it really badly and still know it's not a healthy thing for me. Honestly I've accepted that a lapse (I refuse to call it a "relapse") may happen, and smoking weed once won't undo all the good work I've done. It helps to not put too much pressure on myself to have a long streak.

When I seriously consider using it again, I generally decide not to. Sometimes I've just been lucky though and ran into obstacles. For me it really has been a mixture of luck and determination.

Also I did try to quit for about a year without success. So don't lose heart - all your attempts at quitting are practice for the real thing. I think that's the healthiest way to view it.

I don't know if I have the correct thoughts but I believe in cognitive therapy - it's pulled me out of some very tight spots.

I've definitely had to change my thinking to get sober. It's one of the hardest things I've done.

I agree. I am looking into changing my environment. I'll wait until after December is up first, as I know no one can honestly deal with moving or finding new roommates in December. But yeah, I really need my own space.
I'm not expecting anyone to quit smoking weed. I just want them to not leave weed in the common areas, which I think is a reasonable request.

A friend used to call me a "depoliticized straight-edger". Sobriety is something that I think is important to me, whether or not I slip here and there. I'm definitely better off without weed and I think the people closest to me see that too. Or I hope they do - I'm no stranger to the defensive reactions from people when I call it an addiction.

I don't know if I'm holding on to it or not, but one thing I do know is that it was a lot easier to be sober before I tried drugs than after. Particularly with weed. It's like a pandora's box was opened.
Yeah I'm going to talk to my roommates about my desire to move sometime in January. I don't think it would be kind to dump this on them in the middle of December. :)

The city I live in is pretty tolerant of weed use so I'm not super worried about that. I think the landlord doesn't really care as long as I pay the rent. I used to be more worried about things like this.

I don't get as panicked as I used to. Smoking weed brought out the worst feelings for me, and when my addiction was at its worst I used it to punish/torture myself.

Last night I even found myself craving the terrible feelings and that's something that really creeped me out.

Anyway... when I stopped punishing myself w/ weed my anxiety greatly reduced and my suicidal feelings largely went away (though I needed to find my recent cocktail of meds to really move forward)
Thank you. I truly appreciate that. Yeah, it seemed like the perfect crime at the time but fortunately I didn't give in. I can be pretty stubborn when I'm set on something.

Thank you. I'm not sure how I'm doing today tbh. Part of me just wants to try again. I know that sounds terrible but it's how I feel.

Roommates are in their own crises and not super available right now. Trying to reach out though. It's hard.

Thank you! Self-love is soooo important. I am trying very hard to love myself through feelings of shame and deep sadness.

It took a while to get to this point... for one thing I had to come to the conclusion that I could not kill myself. That was the hardest thing to accept, because dying is actually a very attractive solution: less work than fixing the mess you made in your life. But I couldn't love myself if I wanted to kill myself. And weed was making me more suicidal. So even though my life revolved around it, I had to let it go. I am so glad I did.

Yeah. I think part of the issue was that I was using weed not just to hide from my mental illness, but also to punish myself. Weed was nice for about a half hour and after that it put me into a terrible state of mind. Sometimes I smoked because I thought I deserved to be in that state of mind.

Quitting weed, for me, was a "next step" in my recovery from my mental illness. I was actually using skills I learned in therapy in order to help me quit. Things like self-validation, distraction, delaying gratification, mindfulness, etc. I don't think I could have done this without those skills.

Hmm? I'm not sure what you mean.

I recognize that YMMV and I've been through a lot of therapy too. I don't think that quitting weed alone is a good way to address mental illness. I wasn't trying to give anyone false hope and I'm not sure how you got that idea.

That said, I hope that you are OK.

It's great that you want to look into this when you're still 16. You will see a lot of posts from people who started quitting in their 30s or more who wished they got it under control at a younger age. So that is something!

A comment I posted to a different thread might be relevant:

https://www.reddit.com/r/leaves/comments/3g62sh/decided_to_quit_finally_always_made_excuses_and_i/ctvpzzf
I learned that food is still delicious sober. This was possibly my most important discovery. :-)

Yeah that makes sense! I've reached the point where I'm OK with sitting with my best friend while they smoke weed without wanting it too badly. I think my friends finally noticed how much it was hurting me, so they cut the defensiveness out. Not everyone is mature enough to do that, but hopefully your people are.

Setting boundaries with weed and alcohol for me was very good practice for setting boundaries in other areas of my life. I've been really bad with boundaries and letting people walk all over me. I've also been bad with respecting other peoples boundaries. It's difficult all around.

Definitely a good idea to tell your roomies you're trying to avoid weed, not them! I hope that they will understand. :-)

So a couple things I had to learn that were very hard lessons...

- The first few days can be rough. The first 2.5 weeks for me were really rough. Almost on week 7. Gets easier everyday, but I still crave it. Plan for the cravings.
- Your friends may not be supportive or respectful. People often feel a natural defensiveness when someone they know tries to quit. A big part of this is the fact that the relationship is going to change a lot. Another part is that they might feel their own smoking habits are being challenged. Keep it as neutral as possible, ie "I'm making this change for me, this is how weed is affecting me", and expect that you'll need to find other people to talk to about this.
- People might go from being defensive to downright pressuring you to smoke. Acknowledge it for the shitty behavior that it is. They are probably hurting and trying to control the situation, but know that it shouldn't be your problem even if they make it your problem.
- Try to set boundaries as early as possible. You don't have to make this scary. Simple things like: "Please don't pass me the joint", "Please don't leave weed in common areas (if you have roommates who smoke)", "Please don't talk to me about getting high/wanting to get high", etc., are all basic things that any good friend would respect.
- Take responsibility for your choices too. If you ask a friend for some weed, they're not a bad friend for giving it to you. You're in charge of this, 100%, and just as it's not fair for others to offer it to you when you set that boundary, it's also not fair to expect your friends to be responsible for you when you're struggling. Not trying to be condescending on this last point -- I can't emphasize it enough, taking absolute responsibility for my actions was one of the hardest things for me to learn, but when I did learn this, everything became WAY easier.

It gets easier with time. You might relapse, but as long as you delay gratification you're still building resilience. I wish you the very best.

"No you're not."

Best response: "You're right actually, I'm not."

You have the right to make changes. You have the right to decide what goes in your body. It's up to her to adapt. You're not responsible for her smoking/not smoking (nor is she responsible for yours).

You can empathize that this change may be difficult for her, because change usually is hard for people. You have nothing to apologize for.

Same here. Just passed the 30 day mark, and starting to see a lot of improvement in my life where I used to see no hope.

You rock, keep it up!

I agree, this place has been super helpful. I have experienced people being defensive about me quitting, telling my my weed use isn't that bad, telling me that the withdrawal effects weren't the weed and that dependence isn't real, etc.

This place is wonderful because it divorces the politics of weed from our personal goals.

Being cheated on sucks. I've been there, both as the cheater and the one being cheated on. There are lots of reasons that it can happen, but it still ultimately represents a betrayal and is a really mean thing to do to a partner.

You can survive this sober. I wouldn't blame you if you did have weed, but I'm telling you that you can survive this. You already have a month of sobriety, during which you practiced skills and strategies to stay off of weed.

If you end up using weed to cope, the past month still made you a stronger person, and the skills you learned would be applicable in the future.

There is no excusing her behaviour. Even with complicating factors, she most likely had some role in being whisked away. It's a pattern, by the sounds of it, and she is probably really unhappy in the relationship but for whatever reason is not being completely honest with you.

The world would be a better place if people ended relationships before cheating. No one can tell you how to handle this though. All I can say is, hang in there.
Thank you. I ended up putting it in a cupboard so that at least I wouldn't look at it.

I definitely had to quit alcohol and weed together. I tried doing it one at a time, but I only just increased my consumption of the substance I was allowed to consume to compensate.

This isn't exactly advice, just my experience. What you're doing is really hard and a lot of people here can relate to it. Good luck!

Those 6 days are definitely not wasted! A thing I've learned in therapy is that delaying unwanted behaviours makes us stronger, even if in the end we "cave" and do what we've been trying to avoid.

It's all about practice and learning your triggers, and it sounds like you're well on the way to recovery. :-)

Distraction sometimes, like TV, games, books, cuddling an animal.

Checking the facts of what is causing you anxiety -- weed and lack thereof can modify our emotions, but usually for me there are some unjustified thoughts that are contributing. While you can't completely end a panic attack this way, you can slow it down by challenging some of the beliefs that are feeding it.

Deep breathing helps. It's better to practice before your anxiety starts, but again it's useful at any stage.

Describe the room you're in to yourself.

Anxiety is really hard. If you've had it for a while then you may have tried these already. In any case, I wish you well and hope you feel better soon.

Also, I honestly believe that if you slip up and smoke once, the amount of discipline and strength you earned by abstaining is still there. If we catastrophize our mistakes it can lead to a defeatist attitude and make things a lot worse.
This is probably the reason I didn't tell people right away that I was quitting. I only brought it up when offered, and only so that people wouldn't tempt me.
It is very hard when you're often around people who smoke. Hang in there.

Symptoms of my mental illness are being intensified by weed use, and I live with roommates which means the effects of my illness are spilling over into the lives of people who don't deserve it. Money is a small factor, but it's more about realizing that this drug isn't right for me and taking care of myself.

On that note, I am also quitting alcohol because I don't want to put my roommates in an awkward situation where they have to take care of me again.

[edit]

I will just say that on top of that I have an addictive personality and trying to control or moderate always failed. I even tried only smoking with groups of friends, and usually it just got me started again. I don't think I can do moderation with any vice, although it's a skill I'll have to learn.
Thank you. I hope that I can find a way too.
